title: ROS 2, the Robot Nervous System

mentor.name: TOPIC-1
mentor.character: Teaches by wiring one node at a time and refuses to move on until you can name every edge of the graph.

summary: Build a complete ROS 2 robot in Python, from a single node to a system of drivers, filters, behaviours and a supervisor that brings them up in order. You finish able to write nodes, topics, services, actions, parameters, QoS profiles, launch files, TF2 broadcasters and a URDF, and to debug the running graph with the command line tools and bags.

lessons.title: The Nervous System Wakes
lessons.goal: Start a ROS 2 context from Python, create a node and log a line from it.
lessons.theory:
ROS 2 is not an operating system and not a library you import into one big program. It is middleware: a set of rules and libraries that let many small programs on the same robot talk to each other. Each of those programs is a **node**. On a differential drive base with a Jetson Orin Nano you will typically run one node for the laser, one for the motor driver, one for odometry and one for the behaviour that decides where to go.

ROS 1 had a master process, `roscore`, and if it died the whole robot went blind. ROS 2 has no master. Discovery happens over DDS, the same class of middleware used in aircraft and naval systems. Two nodes on the same network find each other by themselves, which is why you can unplug the laptop and the robot keeps driving.

From Python you talk to all of this through `rclpy`. Before you can create anything you must initialise the context with `rclpy.init()`, and before the process exits you call `rclpy.shutdown()`. Between those two calls you own a node. Every node carries a logger that writes to the console and to the ROS log files under `~/.ros/log`, so use it instead of `print`.

lessons.title: Breathing In the Void
lessons.goal: Keep a node alive with rclpy.spin and exit cleanly on Ctrl-C.
lessons.theory:
A node that reaches the end of `main` dies immediately. That is fine for a one shot script, useless for a laser driver that has to run for hours. To stay alive a node has to be handed to an **executor**, and the simplest way to do that is `rclpy.spin(node)`.

Spin is a blocking loop. It waits for work: a message arriving on a subscription, a timer firing, a service request, a parameter change. When work appears it calls your callback, then goes back to waiting. Nothing in `rclpy` runs your callbacks behind your back. If you never spin, your subscriptions are dead sockets.

Ctrl-C raises `KeyboardInterrupt` inside spin. If you do not catch it, the node object is destroyed by the garbage collector at an unpredictable moment and DDS can print ugly errors on the way out. The pattern used in production packages is a `try` around spin and an explicit `destroy_node` plus `shutdown` afterwards.

    node.get_logger().info('probe online, holding station')

lessons.solution:
import rclpy


def main():
    rclpy.init()
    node = rclpy.create_node('nebula_probe')
    node.get_logger().info('probe online, holding station')
    try:
        rclpy.spin(node)
    except KeyboardInterrupt:
        node.get_logger().info('stop requested, standing down')
    finally:
        node.destroy_node()
        rclpy.shutdown()


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

lessons.title: Blueprint of a Package
lessons.goal: Declare a Python node as an executable of an ament_python package in setup.py.
lessons.theory:
ROS 2 code does not live in loose scripts. It lives in **packages**. A Python package built with `ament_python` has a fixed shape: a `package.xml` with metadata and dependencies, a `setup.py` that installs it, a folder with the same name as the package holding the modules, and a `resource/` marker file so the package index can find it.

The piece that turns a module into something you can launch is the `entry_points` block in `setup.py`. Each line under `console_scripts` maps a command name to `module:function`. After `colcon build` you can run `ros2 run nebula_bringup probe` and ROS 2 will call that function. Without this line the file is just Python on disk and `ros2 run` will not see it.

The name on the left of the equals sign is what the user types. The path on the right is import syntax, not a file path, so it uses dots and no `.py` extension. Get this wrong and the build succeeds while the executable silently does not exist.
lessons.task: Add a console script named `probe` that points at the `main` function of `nebula_bringup/probe.py`, keeping the maintainer fields intact.

lessons.title: The Node Speaks Its Name
lessons.goal: Give a node a namespace and read back its name, namespace and fully qualified name.
lessons.theory:
Every node has a name and a namespace. The name identifies it in the graph, the namespace groups it with others. A node called `laser` in namespace `/front` is `/front/laser` fully qualified, and that string has to be unique on the whole network. Start two nodes with the same fully qualified name and ROS 2 will let you, then both will behave strangely because tools and remappings cannot tell them apart.

Namespaces are how you run the same code twice on one robot. A two arm humanoid launches the same joint driver under `/left_arm` and `/right_arm`, and every topic that node creates is pushed under that namespace automatically. This is the cheapest form of reuse in ROS 2 and it costs one argument.

From Python you pass `namespace=` when creating the node, and you read it back with `get_name`, `get_namespace` and `get_fully_qualified_name`. Those three are the first thing to log when a node starts, because half of the confusion in a running system comes from a node not being where you thought it was.

lessons.title: Reading the Constellation
lessons.goal: Query the ROS graph from inside a node to list the other nodes and topics that exist.
lessons.theory:
The **graph** is the live picture of who is running and who talks to whom. Nodes are the vertices, topics and services are the edges. You do not build the graph, DDS discovery builds it as nodes appear and vanish, and every node can read it.

From the terminal you inspect it with `ros2 node list`, `ros2 topic list` and `ros2 node info /front/laser`. From Python the same information is on the node object: `get_node_names_and_namespaces()` returns the nodes discovered so far, `get_topic_names_and_types()` returns the topics with their message types. This is what `rqt_graph` and the command line tools call underneath.

Discovery is not instantaneous. If you query the graph in the first milliseconds of a process you will see almost nothing, because the DDS participants have not exchanged announcements yet. Real code either waits a moment or polls on a timer, which is exactly what `ros2 node list` does when it seems slow.
lessons.task: Spin the node briefly so discovery can happen, then log how many nodes are visible and log every topic name found in the graph.

    node = rclpy.create_node('constellation_reader')
    rclpy.spin_once(node, timeout_sec=2.0)
    # TODO: read the graph and report nodes and topics
    node.destroy_node()

lessons.title: Casting a Node in Steel
lessons.goal: Write a node as a subclass of rclpy.node.Node instead of a loose script.
lessons.theory:
The script style from chapter 0 does not scale. As soon as a node owns publishers, timers and state, you need somewhere to keep them, and that place is a class. Every real ROS 2 Python node subclasses `rclpy.node.Node` and calls `super().__init__('node_name')` in its constructor.

Inside the class, `self` is the node. `self.get_logger()`, `self.create_timer()`, `self.create_publisher()` are all methods you inherit. Instance attributes hold the state that survives between callbacks, which is the whole point: a wheel odometry node has to remember the last encoder tick, and a local variable in `main` cannot do that.

The `main` function shrinks to four lines: init, build the object, spin, clean up. That shape is identical in every package you will ever open, so a reviewer can skip it and go straight to the class.

lessons.title: The Heartbeat Timer
lessons.goal: Run work periodically inside a node with create_timer.
lessons.theory:
Robots run on a clock. A motor driver has to send a velocity command every 20 ms or the wheels stop, a battery monitor checks the pack once a second. In ROS 2 you never write `while True` with a `sleep` inside a node, because that blocks the executor and every other callback starves. You create a **timer**.

`self.create_timer(period_seconds, callback)` registers a callback with the executor. The executor fires it as close to the period as it can, and if your callback takes longer than the period, the next tick is late rather than run in parallel. That is a feature: it keeps a single threaded node from re-entering its own callback.

Timer periods are floats in seconds, so 50 Hz is `1.0 / 50.0`. Keep the returned timer object on `self` if you plan to cancel it later with `timer.cancel()`, for example when a robot arm reaches its target and stops streaming setpoints.
lessons.task: Give the heartbeat node a 0.5 second timer that logs an increasing counter, storing both the timer and the counter on the node.
lessons.hint: Pass the method itself as the callback, without parentheses, so the executor can call it later.

lessons.title: Signals in the Dark
lessons.goal: Choose log severities and throttle a message that would otherwise flood the console.
lessons.theory:
Logging is the only window you have into a robot that is driving away from you. ROS 2 gives five severities: debug, info, warn, error and fatal. Use info for state changes, warn for something recoverable such as a dropped laser scan, error for a failure that stops the task, and keep debug for the numbers you only want when hunting a bug.

A callback that runs at 50 Hz and logs on every tick produces 3000 lines a minute and hides everything useful. `rclpy` loggers accept `throttle_duration_sec` to rate limit a specific line, and `once=True` to print it exactly one time. A low battery warning at 50 Hz is noise, the same warning once every 5 seconds is information.

The minimum severity is set per node at runtime with `--ros-args --log-level heartbeat:=debug`, so leaving debug lines in the code costs nothing when they are off.
lessons.task: In the tick callback, warn about low voltage no more than once every five seconds and log the raw reading at debug level on every tick.
lessons.hint: throttle_duration_sec is a keyword argument of the logger call itself, not a separate timer.

lessons.title: One Breath at a Time
lessons.goal: Use spin_once with a timeout to drive a node from your own loop.
lessons.theory:
`rclpy.spin` never returns, which is wrong for programs that have their own main loop. A test harness, a GUI or a script that has to talk to a piece of hardware in a blocking way needs to give the executor a slice of time and take control back. That is `rclpy.spin_once(node, timeout_sec=...)`.

`spin_once` processes at most one ready callback and returns. With `timeout_sec=0.0` it returns immediately whether or not there was work, which makes it safe to call inside a fast loop. With a positive timeout it waits up to that long for something to happen, which is how you poll a service response without burning a core.

The rule that does not change: no callback in ROS 2 runs unless some form of spin is running. If a subscription looks dead, the first question is always whether the process is spinning at all.
lessons.task: Replace the blocking spin with your own loop that calls spin_once with a 0.1 second timeout and stops after twenty iterations.
lessons.starter:
import rclpy
from rclpy.node import Node


class Sampler(Node):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('sampler')
        self.timer = self.create_timer(0.05, self.on_tick)
        self.ticks = 0

    def on_tick(self):
        self.ticks += 1


def main():
    rclpy.init()
    node = Sampler()
    # TODO: drive the node yourself for twenty short slices
    node.get_logger().info('collected {} ticks'.format(node.ticks))
    node.destroy_node()
    rclpy.shutdown()


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()
lessons.hint: A plain for loop around spin_once is enough, the timeout keeps each slice short.

lessons.title: Standing Down Cleanly
lessons.goal: Shut a node down without leaving DDS resources or a half open context behind.
lessons.theory:
Shutdown order matters. The node owns DDS entities: publishers, subscriptions, timers, service servers. `destroy_node()` releases them. `rclpy.shutdown()` tears down the context that those entities were created in. Call shutdown first and destroy after, and you get warnings about operating on an invalid context.

There is a second trap. If shutdown already happened, for example because a signal handler ran, calling `rclpy.shutdown()` again raises. Guard it with `rclpy.ok()`, which reports whether the context is still valid. Modern code writes a `finally` block that destroys the node and shuts down only if `rclpy.ok()`.

On a real robot this is not cosmetic. A motor driver node that dies without destroying its subscription can leave the last velocity command latched in a downstream buffer, and the base keeps rolling. Clean shutdown is part of the safety story.
lessons.task: Write the shutdown block so the node is always destroyed and the context is only shut down when it is still valid.
lessons.hint: rclpy.ok() tells you whether the context is still alive, and it belongs in an if around shutdown.

lessons.title: Two Minds, One Process
lessons.goal: Run two nodes in a single process using an explicit executor.
lessons.theory:
`rclpy.spin(node)` is a shortcut that builds a `SingleThreadedExecutor`, adds one node and spins it. Once you want two nodes in one process, you build the executor yourself.

Why would you? Because processes are expensive on an embedded board. A robot with fifteen nodes each in its own process pays fifteen times for the DDS participant, the discovery traffic and the Python interpreter. Grouping the small ones, a battery monitor and a fan controller for example, into one process saves real memory on an Orin Nano.

The pattern is `executor = SingleThreadedExecutor()`, `executor.add_node(a)`, `executor.add_node(b)`, `executor.spin()`. All callbacks from both nodes run on the same thread in turn, so one slow callback still delays the other node. That trade is the subject of the next lesson.
lessons.task: Create both nodes, add them to a single SingleThreadedExecutor and spin it once, then destroy both on the way out.
lessons.starter:
import rclpy
from rclpy.executors import SingleThreadedExecutor
from rclpy.node import Node


class Fan(Node):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('fan')
        self.create_timer(1.0, lambda: self.get_logger().info('fan at 40 percent'))


class Battery(Node):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('battery')
        self.create_timer(1.0, lambda: self.get_logger().info('pack at 11.6 V'))


def main():
    rclpy.init()
    fan = Fan()
    battery = Battery()
    # TODO: run both nodes on one executor
    fan.destroy_node()
    battery.destroy_node()
    rclpy.shutdown()


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()
lessons.hint: Build the executor, add both nodes with add_node, then call spin on the executor and not on rclpy.

lessons.title: Many Hands on the Deck
lessons.goal: Use a MultiThreadedExecutor so a slow callback does not block the rest of the node.
lessons.theory:
A single threaded executor runs one callback at a time. If your image processing callback takes 300 ms, the 50 Hz safety timer that watches the bumper does not run for 300 ms. On a moving robot that is fifteen centimetres of blindness.

`MultiThreadedExecutor` runs callbacks on a pool of threads, by default one per CPU. Two callbacks can then overlap in time. That solves the starvation and creates the classic problem: two threads touching the same attribute of your node. Python's global interpreter lock protects the interpreter, not your data, so a read modify write on a shared counter is still a race.

The executor alone does not decide what may overlap. That is the job of callback groups, which is the next lesson. For now, know that switching to the multi threaded executor is one line and that it changes the concurrency contract of every callback you have already written.
lessons.task: Swap the executor for a MultiThreadedExecutor with four threads and keep the rest of the shutdown sequence intact.
lessons.starter:
import time

import rclpy
from rclpy.executors import SingleThreadedExecutor
from rclpy.node import Node


class Vision(Node):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('vision')
        self.create_timer(0.1, self.heavy)
        self.create_timer(0.02, lambda: self.get_logger().debug('bumper clear'))

    def heavy(self):
        time.sleep(0.3)
        self.get_logger().info('frame processed')


def main():
    rclpy.init()
    node = Vision()
    executor = SingleThreadedExecutor()
    # TODO: use four worker threads instead of one
    executor.add_node(node)
    try:
        executor.spin()
    except KeyboardInterrupt:
        pass
    finally:
        node.destroy_node()
        if rclpy.ok():
            rclpy.shutdown()


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

lessons.title: Who May Run Beside Whom
lessons.goal: Separate callbacks with MutuallyExclusiveCallbackGroup and ReentrantCallbackGroup.
lessons.theory:
A **callback group** is a promise about concurrency. Every callback belongs to one, and the executor honours the group's rule.

`MutuallyExclusiveCallbackGroup` means no two callbacks in that group ever run at the same time. That is the default group of a node, and it is why single threaded code is safe by accident. `ReentrantCallbackGroup` means anything in it may run in parallel with anything else in it, including a second copy of the same callback.

The practical recipe on a robot: put the fast safety timer in its own mutually exclusive group so it never waits behind the slow one, put the slow perception work in another, and reach for reentrant only when a callback has to wait for a service response that another callback of the same node has to deliver. Groups only matter under a multi threaded executor, but writing them down documents the intent even before you switch.
lessons.task: Give the safety timer and the perception timer each their own MutuallyExclusiveCallbackGroup so they can overlap under the multi threaded executor.

lessons.title: The Node's Own Clock
lessons.goal: Read time from the node clock and measure an elapsed Duration.
lessons.theory:
Never call `time.time()` inside a ROS 2 node. The node has its own clock, `self.get_clock()`, and it is the one that follows simulation time. When you launch with `use_sim_time` true, that clock is driven by the `/clock` topic that Gazebo publishes, so your node slows down and speeds up with the simulator. Python's wall clock does not.

`self.get_clock().now()` returns a `rclpy.time.Time`. Subtracting two of them gives a `Duration`, whose `nanoseconds` field is an integer. Divide by `1e9` for seconds. To stamp a message you convert with `.to_msg()`, which produces the `builtin_interfaces/Time` that goes inside a header.

This is also how you write timeouts that behave in simulation: capture a start time, and on every tick compare `now - start` against a `Duration(seconds=5)`. A `sleep` inside a callback would block the executor and ignore sim time twice over.
lessons.task: Store the start time in the constructor and, on each tick, log how many seconds have passed according to the node clock.
lessons.hint: Subtracting two Time objects gives a Duration, and its nanoseconds field is an integer.

lessons.title: First Words on the Wire
lessons.goal: Create a publisher and send a std_msgs/String message onto a topic.
lessons.theory:
A **topic** is a named stream of messages. Publishers write to it, subscribers read from it, and neither knows the other exists. That anonymity is the reason you can swap a real laser for a simulated one without touching the node that consumes the scan.

`self.create_publisher(msg_type, topic_name, qos_depth)` returns a publisher. The message type is a Python class generated from an interface definition, imported from the package that owns it, for example `from std_msgs.msg import String`. The third argument is the queue depth, a number of messages to keep buffered for slow subscribers. Ten is the usual default.

You never build the wire format yourself. You instantiate the message class, fill its fields, and call `publisher.publish(msg)`. A `std_msgs/String` has exactly one field, `data`, and it must be a Python `str`. Assigning an int there raises immediately, which is the type system doing its job.
lessons.task: Create a publisher of std_msgs/String on the topic `status` with depth 10, and publish one message with the text of your choice from the constructor.
lessons.hint: Build an empty String(), assign its data field, then hand it to publish.

lessons.title: A Steady Pulse of Data
lessons.goal: Publish at a fixed rate by driving the publisher from a timer.
lessons.theory:
Publishing once from the constructor is almost always a bug. At that moment no subscriber has discovered you yet, so the message goes nowhere. Sensor data, odometry and velocity commands are streams, and streams come from timers.

The standard shape of a driver node is: a publisher and a timer created in the constructor, and a callback that reads the hardware, fills a message and publishes it. A YDLIDAR X4 spins at 7 Hz, a wheel encoder loop runs at 50 Hz, a `cmd_vel` stream to a differential base is normally 20 Hz. Pick the period from the device, not from habit.

Keep the message construction inside the callback. Reusing one message object across ticks looks efficient and bites you the first time a field is left over from the previous iteration.
lessons.task: Publish a String on `status` at 5 Hz from a timer, including a counter that increases on every message.
lessons.solution:
import rclpy
from rclpy.node import Node
from std_msgs.msg import String


class Talker(Node):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('talker')
        self.pub = self.create_publisher(String, 'status', 10)
        self.seq = 0
        self.timer = self.create_timer(1.0 / 5.0, self.on_tick)

    def on_tick(self):
        self.seq += 1
        msg = String()
        msg.data = 'base ready, frame {}'.format(self.seq)
        self.pub.publish(msg)


def main():
    rclpy.init()
    node = Talker()
    try:
        rclpy.spin(node)
    except KeyboardInterrupt:
        pass
    finally:
        node.destroy_node()
        if rclpy.ok():
            rclpy.shutdown()


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()
lessons.hint: 5 Hz is a period of 1.0 / 5.0 seconds, and the message has to be built inside the callback.

lessons.title: The Ear on the Bus
lessons.goal: Subscribe to a topic and react to every message in a callback.
lessons.theory:
`self.create_subscription(msg_type, topic, callback, qos_depth)` is the mirror of a publisher. The callback receives one argument, the message, already deserialised into a Python object. It runs on the executor, so a slow callback delays everything else in its group.

The type has to match. If the publisher sends `std_msgs/String` and you subscribe with `std_msgs/Int32`, the two endpoints simply do not connect and you get silence, no error. `ros2 topic info /status --verbose` shows both sides and their types, and it is the first command to run when nothing arrives.

Keep the subscription object on `self`. If you let it be garbage collected the subscription is destroyed and the topic goes quiet, which is a classic hour lost. The common convention is `self.sub = self.create_subscription(...)`.
lessons.task: Subscribe to `status` with depth 10 and log the received text, keeping the subscription alive on the node.
lessons.hint: The argument order is type, topic, callback, depth, and the result must be stored on self.

lessons.title: Commanding the Wheels
lessons.goal: Publish a geometry_msgs/Twist on cmd_vel to drive a differential base.
lessons.theory:
`cmd_vel` is the most standardised topic in ROS 2. Nearly every mobile base, from a TurtleBot 4 to a custom rover with RoboClaw drivers, subscribes to `geometry_msgs/Twist` on that name. If your node publishes a correct Twist, it can drive hardware it has never seen.

A `Twist` has two `Vector3` fields, `linear` and `angular`, each with `x`, `y` and `z`. A differential drive robot can only use `linear.x` in metres per second and `angular.z` in radians per second. Everything else is ignored by the driver because the wheels physically cannot produce it. A holonomic base with mecanum wheels also uses `linear.y`.

Safety detail that costs robots: the driver keeps applying the last command it received. If your node stops publishing while the robot is moving, most drivers hold the velocity until a watchdog fires. Always publish an explicit zero Twist when you stop.
lessons.task: Publish a Twist on `cmd_vel` at 20 Hz that drives forward at 0.25 m/s while turning left at 0.4 rad/s.
lessons.hint: Forward speed is linear.x and yaw rate is angular.z, both floats.

lessons.title: The Sweep of the Laser
lessons.goal: Read a sensor_msgs/LaserScan and extract the distance straight ahead.
lessons.theory:
A `sensor_msgs/LaserScan` is not a list of points, it is a polar sweep. The fields that matter are `angle_min`, `angle_max`, `angle_increment` and the `ranges` array. Range index `i` corresponds to angle `angle_min + i * angle_increment`, measured in the frame named in `header.frame_id`.

To find the beam pointing straight ahead you compute the index of angle zero: `int((0.0 - angle_min) / angle_increment)`. On an RPLIDAR A1 with `angle_min` around minus pi and 360 samples that lands near index 180. Never hardcode the index, different lasers order their sweep differently and some mount backwards.

Invalid returns are not zero, they are `inf` or `nan`. A surface that absorbs the beam or is closer than `range_min` produces them. Filter with `math.isfinite` before you feed the number to an obstacle check, otherwise a `nan` comparison silently evaluates false and your robot decides the corridor is clear.
lessons.task: In the callback, compute the index of the forward beam, guard against non finite values, and log the distance ahead.
lessons.hint: The index of angle zero is (0 - angle_min) / angle_increment, and math.isfinite rejects inf and nan.

lessons.title: Stamping the Moment
lessons.goal: Fill a std_msgs/Header with a frame id and a timestamp from the node clock.
lessons.theory:
Any message that describes something physical carries a `std_msgs/Header` with two fields you must fill: `stamp` and `frame_id`. Without them the data is unusable. A distance of 1.2 m means nothing until you know it was measured at time t from the frame `laser_link`.

`frame_id` is the name of the coordinate frame the data is expressed in. It is what TF2 uses later to move that measurement into the robot base or into the map. `stamp` is a `builtin_interfaces/Time`, and you get a correct one with `self.get_clock().now().to_msg()`. Using the wall clock here breaks everything the moment you replay a bag or run in simulation.

Stamp at acquisition, not at publication. If you read a sensor over serial and the parse takes 8 ms, stamping after the parse pushes every downstream transform 8 ms into the future. On a robot turning at 1 rad/s that is half a degree of error injected for free.
lessons.task: Fill the header of the PointStamped with the frame `laser_link` and the current node time, then publish it.
lessons.solution:
import rclpy
from geometry_msgs.msg import PointStamped
from rclpy.node import Node


class Beacon(Node):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('beacon')
        self.pub = self.create_publisher(PointStamped, 'target', 10)
        self.timer = self.create_timer(0.5, self.on_tick)

    def on_tick(self):
        msg = PointStamped()
        msg.header.stamp = self.get_clock().now().to_msg()
        msg.header.frame_id = 'laser_link'
        msg.point.x = 1.2
        self.pub.publish(msg)


def main():
    rclpy.init()
    node = Beacon()
    try:
        rclpy.spin(node)
    except KeyboardInterrupt:
        pass
    finally:
        node.destroy_node()
        if rclpy.ok():
            rclpy.shutdown()


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()
lessons.hint: to_msg turns the node clock time into the type the header expects.

lessons.title: Forging a New Message
lessons.goal: Define a custom .msg interface and declare the generator in CMakeLists.
lessons.theory:
When no existing message fits, you define your own. Interface definitions live in a package of their own, built with `ament_cmake` even if all your nodes are Python, because the code generator `rosidl` runs from CMake.

A `.msg` file is a list of `type name` lines. Primitive types are `bool`, `int8` to `int64`, `float32`, `float64` and `string`. You can nest other messages by their full name, `std_msgs/Header header`, and declare arrays with `float64[] values` or fixed size with `float64[4] quaternion`. Constants use the form `uint8 MODE_IDLE=0`.

The package needs `rosidl_default_generators` as a build dependency, the `rosidl_generate_interfaces` call listing every file, and `<member_of_group>rosidl_interface_packages</member_of_group>` in `package.xml`. Forget the last one and your Python nodes will import the message and fail at runtime with a missing type support error.
lessons.task: Write the CMake block that generates the interfaces for `msg/WheelState.msg`, which carries a header, a float64 velocity and a float64 current.

lessons.title: Listening from the Terminal
lessons.goal: Inspect a live topic with the ros2 topic commands and reproduce their output from a node.
lessons.theory:
Before you write a subscriber, interrogate the topic. `ros2 topic list` shows what exists. `ros2 topic info /scan --verbose` shows the type and every publisher and subscriber with its QoS. `ros2 topic echo /scan` prints messages as YAML. `ros2 topic hz /scan` measures the real rate, which is how you discover that your 10 Hz laser is actually delivering 6 Hz over a saturated wifi link.

`ros2 topic pub` is the other half. `ros2 topic pub /cmd_vel geometry_msgs/msg/Twist "{linear: {x: 0.2}}" --once` moves a robot without writing a line of code, and `--rate 10` keeps it moving. This is the fastest way to test a motor driver in isolation.

From Python the same measurement is a subscription that keeps timestamps. Counting messages over a window and dividing gives you the rate, which is what a health monitor node publishes so you can see a starving sensor on a dashboard instead of in a terminal.
lessons.task: Count the messages received on `scan` and, once per second, log the measured rate in hertz.
lessons.hint: The subscription callback only increments, the timer reports and then zeroes the counter.

lessons.title: Rewiring Without Rewriting
lessons.goal: Understand topic remapping and write nodes with relative topic names so they can be moved.
lessons.theory:
Hardcoding `/scan` with a leading slash pins a node to one absolute name forever. Writing `scan` without the slash makes it **relative**, so it resolves under the node namespace: the same node launched in `/front` publishes `/front/scan` and in `/rear` publishes `/rear/scan`. This is the difference between code you can run twice and code you cannot.

On top of namespaces there is **remapping**. `ros2 run nebula_bringup pilot --ros-args -r cmd_vel:=/base/cmd_vel_safe` rewires the topic at launch time without recompiling. Node names can be remapped too with `-r __node:=pilot_left`, and the namespace with `-r __ns:=/left`.

The rule to work by: always write relative names in code, and let the launch file decide the absolute wiring. A driver that insists on `/cmd_vel` cannot sit behind a safety filter, because the filter needs to own that name and hand the driver a different one.
lessons.task: Rewrite the pilot so both its subscription and its publisher use relative names, `scan` in and `cmd_vel` out, and log the resolved names at startup.
lessons.hint: Drop the leading slash from both names, and the resolved name is available as topic_name on the publisher and the subscription.

lessons.title: Laying the Keel
lessons.goal: Build a colcon workspace and understand what src, build, install and log hold.
lessons.theory:
A **workspace** is a folder with a `src/` inside it and nothing else that you write by hand. You clone or create packages under `src`, run `colcon build` from the workspace root, and colcon creates three siblings: `build/` with intermediate artefacts, `install/` with what actually gets used, and `log/` with the record of each build.

`colcon build --symlink-install` is the flag you want for Python packages. Without it, every edit to a `.py` file requires a rebuild to be copied into `install/`. With it, the installed file is a symlink back to your source, so you edit and rerun. It does not help with new entry points or changed `setup.py`, those still need a rebuild.

Build one package at a time while iterating with `colcon build --packages-select nebula_bringup`. On a full robot workspace with thirty packages a blind rebuild is several minutes you will spend many times a day.
lessons.task: Write a shell function that creates the workspace layout and builds only the bringup package with symlink install.
lessons.hint: Two flags on colcon build: one for symlinks, one to select a single package.

lessons.title: The Manifest of the Ship
lessons.goal: Declare a package and its runtime dependencies in package.xml.
lessons.theory:
`package.xml` is the manifest every ROS 2 package must have. It gives the package a name, a version, a licence, a maintainer, and the list of packages it needs. Tools read it: `rosdep` to install system dependencies, `colcon` to order the build, the package index to find the package at runtime.

There are three dependency kinds that matter. `<depend>` means needed both to build and to run, and is what you use for `rclpy`, `sensor_msgs` and your own interface package. `<exec_depend>` is runtime only, typical for a Python package that just imports something. `<build_depend>` is build only, mostly for CMake packages.

The build type at the bottom decides everything else. `<build_type>ament_python</build_type>` inside `<export>` tells colcon to run `setup.py`. Put `ament_cmake` there by mistake in a Python package and the build fails with a missing CMakeLists error that says nothing about the real cause.
lessons.task: Complete the manifest so the package depends on rclpy, sensor_msgs and geometry_msgs, and is built as an ament_python package.

lessons.title: Naming the Crew
lessons.goal: Expose several nodes of one package as separate ros2 run executables.
lessons.theory:
One package normally holds several nodes. The laser driver, the odometry publisher and the safety filter of the same robot belong together, and each one needs its own entry point.

Every line in `console_scripts` is independent, so a package with three nodes has three lines pointing at three modules. The command names live in a flat namespace per package, which means `ros2 run nebula_bringup pilot` is unambiguous even if another package also has a `pilot`.

After adding an entry point you must rebuild, even with `--symlink-install`, because the console script wrapper is generated at install time. If `ros2 run` says the executable was not found and the file is clearly there, that missing rebuild is the reason nine times out of ten.
lessons.task: Expose three executables of the bringup package: `pilot`, `laser_driver` and `odom_publisher`, each pointing at the main of the module with the same name.
lessons.hint: Copy the shape of the first line and change both sides of the equals sign.

lessons.title: Calling the Suppliers
lessons.goal: Resolve system and ROS dependencies of a workspace with rosdep.
lessons.theory:
`rosdep` reads every `package.xml` in your workspace and installs what is missing. It maps a ROS key such as `sensor_msgs` or a system key such as `python3-serial` to the actual apt package for your distribution. This is why a correct manifest matters beyond documentation: it is executable.

The two commands are `rosdep update`, which refreshes the key database, and `rosdep install --from-paths src --ignore-src -r -y` from the workspace root. `--ignore-src` tells it not to try installing packages you have in source, `-r` continues past errors, `-y` answers yes.

When a key is missing entirely, rosdep fails with the key name. Either the dependency is misspelled, or it is a pip only package that needs an entry in a rosdep yaml. Adding an undeclared import and shipping it works on your machine and breaks on the robot, which is the single most common way a ROS 2 deployment fails.
lessons.task: Return the two command lines that update the rosdep database and install every dependency declared in the workspace source folder without prompting.
lessons.hint: The install command points at src and needs the flag that skips packages already present in source.

lessons.title: Layers of the Sky
lessons.goal: Explain overlays and sourcing order, and detect which workspace a node was loaded from.
lessons.theory:
Sourcing `/opt/ros/humble/setup.bash` gives you the **underlay**, the distribution. Sourcing `~/nebula_ws/install/setup.bash` afterwards adds your **overlay** on top. If a package name exists in both, the overlay wins. That is how you patch a system package without touching the system.

Order is not symmetric. Source the overlay first and the underlay second and you get the system version, which produces the classic report of a fix that works for one engineer and not another. The safe habit is one line in the shell for the underlay and one for the overlay, always in that order, and never sourcing two different overlays into the same shell.

From Python you can see where a package came from with `ament_index_python.get_package_share_directory`. Printing that path at startup turns a confusing bug into a one line answer, because the path says whether you are running the code you just edited.
lessons.task: Log the share directory of the running package and handle the case where the package is not found.

lessons.title: The Inspector's Toolbelt
lessons.goal: Map each ros2 command line verb to the graph concept it inspects.
lessons.theory:
The `ros2` command is a family, and every branch of it has the same shape: `ros2`, the concept, then a verb. `ros2 node list` and `ros2 node info` cover nodes. `ros2 topic list` and `ros2 topic info` cover streams. `ros2 service list` covers request and reply, `ros2 action list` covers the long tasks, `ros2 param list` covers configuration, and `ros2 interface show` prints the definition of any message, service or action type.

Two of them save whole afternoons. `ros2 interface show sensor_msgs/msg/LaserScan` prints the exact field list so you stop guessing names. `ros2 doctor --report` dumps the middleware in use, the domain id and the network interfaces, which is what you check first when two machines cannot see each other.

The domain id deserves its own note. `ROS_DOMAIN_ID` partitions the network. Two robots on the same wifi with the same domain id will see each other's topics and fight over `cmd_vel`. Different id, invisible to each other, and no error message either way.
lessons.task: Complete the lookup table so services, actions, parameters and interface definitions each map to the command that inspects them.

    'node': 'ros2 node list',

lessons.title: Drawing the Constellation
lessons.goal: Detect a topic that has publishers but no subscribers by querying the graph counts.
lessons.theory:
`rqt_graph` draws the running system as a picture. It is the fastest way to see that two nodes you thought were connected are actually publishing to two different topic names, one with a typo. The picture comes from the same graph API you used in chapter 0.

The counts are the useful part in code. `count_publishers(topic)` and `count_subscribers(topic)` return integers for any topic name, whether or not the node itself is connected to it. A publisher with zero subscribers is data thrown away, a subscriber with zero publishers is a node waiting forever.

A health node that checks these counts at startup catches wiring mistakes before the robot moves. This is more reliable than reading a launch file, because it reports what actually resolved after namespaces and remappings were applied.
lessons.task: Once per second, log the publisher and subscriber count of `cmd_vel` and warn when nobody is listening.
lessons.hint: Both counting methods live on the node and take the resolved topic name as a string.

lessons.title: The Flight Recorder
lessons.goal: Record and replay topics with ros2 bag to debug a run that already happened.
lessons.theory:
A **bag** is a recording of messages with their timestamps. `ros2 bag record /scan /odom /cmd_vel` writes an sqlite3 file plus a metadata yaml. `ros2 bag record -a` records everything, which on a robot with cameras fills a disk in minutes, so name your topics.

`ros2 bag play nebula_run` republishes those messages with the original timing, so every node downstream sees exactly what it saw during the run. `ros2 bag info nebula_run` prints duration, message counts and types. This is how robotics debugging actually works: you do not reproduce the failure on the robot, you replay the bag into the node you are fixing.

One condition makes replay honest. Nodes must run with `use_sim_time` true and the bag must be played with `--clock`, so that everyone's clock comes from the recording rather than from the wall. Without it, a node that timestamps its own output mixes recorded time with present time and TF2 rejects the result.
lessons.task: Return the three command lines that record the three topics into `nebula_run`, inspect the result, and replay it publishing the clock.
lessons.hint: The output name is set with -o on record, and the clock flag belongs to play.

lessons.title: Reading the Black Box
lessons.goal: Open a bag from Python with rosbag2_py and deserialise its messages.
lessons.theory:
Sometimes replaying is not enough and you want the numbers. `rosbag2_py` opens a bag directly. You build a `SequentialReader`, open it with a `StorageOptions` pointing at the folder and a `ConverterOptions`, then call `read_next()` until `has_next()` is false.

Each read returns a tuple of topic name, serialised bytes and timestamp in nanoseconds. The bytes are not a Python object yet. You look up the type name in `reader.get_all_topics_and_types()`, resolve the class with `rosidl_runtime_py.utilities.get_message`, and call `rclpy.serialization.deserialize_message`.

This is how you produce a plot of commanded versus measured velocity from a five minute test drive, or count how many scans arrived late. It runs offline with no ROS graph at all, which makes it perfect for a script in continuous integration that checks a regression never comes back.

import rosbag2_py


def count_odom(bag_path):
    reader = rosbag2_py.SequentialReader()
    storage = rosbag2_py.StorageOptions(uri=bag_path, storage_id='sqlite3')
    converter = rosbag2_py.ConverterOptions('', '')
    reader.open(storage, converter)
    total = 0
    while reader.has_next():
        topic, data, stamp = reader.read_next()
        if topic == '/odom':
            total += 1
    return total


print(count_odom('nebula_run'))
lessons.hint: read_next returns topic, raw bytes and timestamp, and the loop runs while has_next is true.

lessons.title: Ask and Be Answered
lessons.goal: Serve a ROS 2 service and fill its response from the request.
lessons.theory:
A topic is a broadcast with no answer. A **service** is a request and one reply, addressed to a specific node. Use it for questions and for short commands: reset the odometry, read the firmware version, compute an inverse kinematics solution. Do not use it for streams and do not use it for anything that takes seconds, that is what actions are for.

A service type has two halves separated by three dashes in the `.srv` file: the request fields and the response fields. `example_interfaces/srv/AddTwoInts` has `int64 a` and `int64 b` in, `int64 sum` out. The generated Python class exposes them as `Request` and `Response`.

`self.create_service(srv_type, name, callback)` registers the server. The callback receives `(request, response)`, an already built empty response, and must return it. Forgetting the return leaves the client hanging forever with no error on either side, which is the signature failure of a first service.
lessons.task: Serve `add_two_ints` so it fills the sum and logs both operands.
lessons.hint: The response object arrives already built, you only assign its fields and return it.

lessons.title: The Client at the Window
lessons.goal: Call a service asynchronously and read the result from the future.
lessons.theory:
`self.create_client(srv_type, name)` builds the caller. Calls are asynchronous: `client.call_async(request)` returns a `Future` immediately, it does not block. The future is filled by the executor when the reply arrives, which means someone has to be spinning for it ever to complete.

The simplest safe way to wait in a script is `rclpy.spin_until_future_complete(node, future)`. It spins the node and returns as soon as the future is done, and it accepts a `timeout_sec` so a dead server does not hang your process forever. After it returns, check `future.done()` before touching `future.result()`.

Never call `client.call()`, the blocking variant, from inside a callback. It waits for a reply that only the executor can deliver, and the executor is busy running your callback. That deadlock is the most reported bug in rclpy and lesson five of this chapter is about escaping it.

import rclpy
from example_interfaces.srv import AddTwoInts

lessons.title: Waiting for the Door to Open
lessons.goal: Block until a service server is available before sending the first request.
lessons.theory:
Nodes start in an unpredictable order. A client created half a second before its server exists will send a request into nothing. Discovery is asynchronous, so the topic of failure here is timing, not correctness.

`client.wait_for_service(timeout_sec=1.0)` returns `True` when the server is discovered and `False` on timeout. The pattern in every well behaved node is a loop that waits in short slices and logs a warning each time, so an operator watching the console sees which dependency is missing instead of a frozen process.

Decide what happens when it never appears. A calibration tool can exit with an error. A safety node must not: it should keep waiting and refuse to let the robot move until the service it depends on is up. Silence in this situation is what turns a missing node into a crashed robot.

lessons.title: A Service of Your Own
lessons.goal: Define a custom .srv interface with request and response halves.
lessons.theory:
A `.srv` file lives in `srv/` inside an interface package and is split by a line of exactly three dashes. Everything above is the request, everything below is the response. The generator produces `Package.srv.Name.Request` and `.Response` classes plus the type support the middleware needs.

Design the response to carry a verdict, not just data. The convention followed by `std_srvs/Trigger` is `bool success` and `string message`. A caller can branch on the boolean, and a human reading the log gets the reason. A service that answers only with a number leaves the client unable to distinguish a real zero from a failure.

Register the file in `rosidl_generate_interfaces` exactly like a message, in the same call, and remember that a package can hold messages, services and actions together. Keeping all interfaces of a robot in one `nebula_interfaces` package avoids the circular dependency you create when two node packages need each other's types.

lessons.title: The Deadlock in the Hall
lessons.goal: Call a service from inside a callback without blocking the executor.
lessons.theory:
Here is the trap. Your subscription callback needs an answer from a service. You call `spin_until_future_complete` inside it. The executor thread is already running your callback, so it cannot process the reply, so the future never completes and the node freezes with no error at all.

There are two correct escapes. The first is to not wait: call `call_async` and attach a completion callback with `future.add_done_callback(self.on_reply)`. Your callback returns immediately, the executor delivers the reply later, and the work continues in `on_reply`. This is the right answer in almost every case.

The second is a `MultiThreadedExecutor` with the caller and the client in different `ReentrantCallbackGroup` groups, so a second thread can process the reply while the first waits. It works, it costs you real concurrency and real locks, and it should be the exception rather than the habit.

lessons.hint: add_done_callback on the future lets the callback return immediately.

lessons.title: Knocking from the Shell
lessons.goal: Call and inspect a service from the command line without writing a client.
lessons.theory:
`ros2 service list` shows every service in the graph, including the six parameter services every node exposes automatically. `ros2 service type /add_two_ints` gives the type, and `ros2 interface show example_interfaces/srv/AddTwoInts` gives the fields.

`ros2 service call` sends a real request with a YAML payload: `ros2 service call /add_two_ints example_interfaces/srv/AddTwoInts "{a: 41, b: 1}"`. The reply prints in the terminal. This is how you test a server before writing any client, and how you trigger a one off action on a robot in the field.

The YAML has to match the field names exactly. A typo produces an empty field with the default value rather than an error, so a request that looks correct can silently send zeros. Reading the interface first is not optional.

lessons.title: The Kill Switch
lessons.goal: Use std_srvs Trigger and SetBool for enable and disable commands.
lessons.theory:
Not every command needs a custom type. `std_srvs` ships three that cover most of a robot: `Empty` for a command with no arguments and no answer, `Trigger` for a command that answers `success` and `message`, and `SetBool` for an on or off switch that answers the same pair.

Using the standard types buys you interoperability. Any operator dashboard, any test script, `ros2 service call` itself, all already know how to speak `SetBool`. Inventing `EnableMotors.srv` with the identical fields buys you nothing and forces every caller to depend on your interface package.

The `message` field is where you put the reason for a refusal. A `SetBool` that returns `success: false` with an empty message is a dead end for whoever is debugging at three in the morning. Write the reason: which interlock is open, which parameter is out of range.

import rclpy
from rclpy.node import Node
from std_srvs.srv import SetBool


class MotorGate(Node):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('motor_gate')
        self.estop = True
        self.enabled = False
        self.srv = self.create_service(SetBool, 'enable_motors', self.on_request)

    def on_request(self, request, response):
        if request.data and self.estop:
            response.success = False
            response.message = 'estop is engaged, release it before enabling the motors'
            return response
        self.enabled = request.data
        response.success = True
        response.message = 'motors {}'.format('enabled' if self.enabled else 'disabled')
        return response


def main():
    rclpy.init()
    node = MotorGate()
    try:
        rclpy.spin(node)
    except KeyboardInterrupt:
        pass
    finally:
        node.destroy_node()
        if rclpy.ok():
            rclpy.shutdown()


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()
lessons.hint: SetBool carries the desired state in request.data and expects success plus message back.

lessons.title: Choosing the Right Channel
lessons.goal: Decide between topic, service and action for a given robot interaction.
lessons.theory:
Three channels, three shapes of problem. A **topic** is for data that flows: sensor readings, velocity commands, state estimates. Many to many, no answer, drop tolerant.

A **service** is for a question with a short answer or a command that completes immediately: read the firmware version, reset odometry to zero, switch the controller mode. One to one, blocking in spirit, and if it takes more than a fraction of a second it is the wrong tool.

An **action** is for work that takes time and can be cancelled: navigate to a pose, pick an object, calibrate the arm. It gives you feedback while it runs, a result at the end, and a cancel path. The mistake that costs the most is implementing navigation as a service, because the caller then has no way to abort a robot heading into a wall.

lessons.title: Defining a Long Task
lessons.goal: Write an .action interface with its goal, result and feedback sections.
lessons.theory:
An **action** is the channel for work that takes time. It is built on top of topics and services: a goal service, a cancel service, a result service and two topics for feedback and status. You never touch those, `rclpy.action` hides them.

An `.action` file has three sections separated by two lines of three dashes. First the goal, what you ask for. Then the result, what you get when it finishes. Then the feedback, what is published periodically while it runs. `nav2_msgs/action/NavigateToPose` asks for a pose, returns an empty result and feeds back the distance remaining.

Design feedback so an operator can tell progress from a stall. Distance remaining plus elapsed time is enough to know whether the robot is stuck. A feedback message with only a percentage that jumps from zero to a hundred is decoration.

lessons.title: The Errand Runner
lessons.goal: Create an ActionServer and finish a goal with succeed and a result.
lessons.theory:
`ActionServer(node, action_type, name, execute_callback)` registers the server. The execute callback receives a `ServerGoalHandle`, reads the request from `goal_handle.request`, does the work, and must end by calling exactly one of `goal_handle.succeed()`, `goal_handle.abort()` or `goal_handle.canceled()`, then returning a result object.

The result class is nested in the action type: `DriveDistance.Result()`. Returning it without calling one of those three methods leaves the goal in an executing state forever, and every client waiting on it hangs.

The execute callback runs on the executor like any other callback, so a long loop inside it blocks everything in its callback group. Real action servers either put themselves in a reentrant group under a multi threaded executor, or step the work forward from a timer and keep the callback short. This chapter uses the first approach for clarity.

lessons.title: Reports from the Road
lessons.goal: Publish feedback from an action server while the goal is running.
lessons.theory:
Feedback is what separates an action from a slow service. `goal_handle.publish_feedback(msg)` sends a `Type.Feedback()` to every client watching this goal. It is a normal topic underneath, so it is best effort in spirit: a client that misses one feedback message is not broken.

Publish at a rate a human can read, one to ten hertz. A navigation server that feeds back at 100 Hz floods the network and tells the operator nothing more than 5 Hz would.

Feedback belongs to a goal, not to the server. If two goals were accepted, each handle publishes its own. Clients receive only the feedback of the goal they sent, which is why the feedback callback on the client side is registered per goal rather than per action.

lessons.title: Sending the Errand

lessons.theory:
`ActionClient(node, action_type, name)` builds the caller. `client.wait_for_server()` blocks until the server is discovered, same reasoning as with services. `client.send_goal_async(goal_msg, feedback_callback=...)` returns a future that resolves to a **goal handle**, not to the result.

The feedback callback receives a wrapper with a `.feedback` field holding your message. It runs on the executor like everything else, so keep it cheap. Logging one line per feedback is fine, replanning a trajectory in there is not.

lessons.title: Accepted or Turned Away
lessons.goal: Check whether a goal was accepted and then wait for its result.
lessons.theory:
A server is allowed to reject a goal. `goal_future.result()` gives you a goal handle with `handle.accepted` as a boolean. If it is false, there is no result coming and any code that waits for one waits forever.

When accepted, ask for the result with `handle.get_result_async()`, which returns the second future. Its result has two fields: `status`, one of the constants of `action_msgs.msg.GoalStatus`, and `result`, your action result message.

The constant you compare against is `GoalStatus.STATUS_SUCCEEDED`, the only status that means the server finished the work it accepted. Its neighbours are `GoalStatus.STATUS_ABORTED`, which the server sets when it gave up halfway, and `GoalStatus.STATUS_CANCELED`, which appears when someone cancelled the goal while it was running. All three deliver a result object, so code that reads `result` without reading `status` first learns nothing about whether the job was actually done.

Write the client so every branch is handled: rejected, aborted, cancelled, succeeded. A navigation client that assumes success is how a robot reports arriving at a goal it never reached.

lessons.title: Calling the Robot Back
lessons.goal: Handle cancellation on the server side and stop the work cleanly.
lessons.theory:
Cancellation is the reason actions exist. The client calls `handle.cancel_goal_async()`, and on the server side the running goal handle reports `goal_handle.is_cancel_requested`. Your execute callback has to check that flag in its loop.

When you see the request, stop the hardware first and only then call `goal_handle.canceled()` and return a result. On a mobile base that means publishing a zero `Twist` before returning, otherwise the driver keeps the last commanded velocity and the robot cancels the goal while still driving.

The server must also accept cancel requests at all. `ActionServer` takes a `cancel_callback` that returns `CancelResponse.ACCEPT` or `REJECT`. The default rejects, which is why a first action server often ignores Ctrl-C on the client and keeps going.

from nebula_interfaces.action import DriveDistance

            self,
            DriveDistance,
            'drive_distance',
            self.execute,
            cancel_callback=self.on_cancel,

                result.completed = False
                result.travelled_m = travelled
                return result
            travelled += target / 50.0
            time.sleep(0.1)
        goal_handle.succeed()
        result.completed = True
        result.travelled_m = travelled
        return result


def main():

    node = Driver()
    try:
        rclpy.spin(node)
    except KeyboardInterrupt:
        pass
    finally:
        node.destroy_node()

lessons.title: One Errand at a Time
lessons.goal: Reject a new goal while another is running using a goal_callback.
lessons.theory:
By default an `ActionServer` accepts every goal, and under a multi threaded executor two goals can run at once. For a robot with one base and one set of wheels that is nonsense: two goals fighting over `cmd_vel` produce motion neither one asked for.

`goal_callback` runs before the goal is accepted and returns `GoalResponse.ACCEPT` or `GoalResponse.REJECT`. Keeping a flag or a reference to the active handle lets you reject anything that arrives while you are busy, and the client learns immediately instead of timing out.

The other policy is preemption: accept the new goal and abort the old one. Nav2 does this, because a newer navigation goal usually supersedes the old one. Both policies are valid, but you must pick one deliberately and the client has to know which it is talking to.
lessons.task: Reject any goal that arrives while another is executing, and free the slot when the goal finishes.

import time

import rclpy
from nebula_interfaces.action import DriveDistance
from rclpy.action import ActionServer, GoalResponse
from rclpy.node import Node


class Driver(Node):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('drive_server')
        self.busy = False
        self.server = ActionServer(
            self,
            DriveDistance,
            'drive_distance',
            self.execute,
            goal_callback=self.on_goal,
        )

    def on_goal(self, goal_request):
        if self.busy:
            self.get_logger().warn('already driving, rejecting the new goal')
            return GoalResponse.REJECT
        return GoalResponse.ACCEPT

    def execute(self, goal_handle):
        self.busy = True
        try:
            time.sleep(1.0)
            goal_handle.succeed()
            result = DriveDistance.Result()
            result.completed = True
            result.travelled_m = goal_handle.request.distance_m
            return result
        finally:
            self.busy = False


def main():
    rclpy.init()
    node = Driver()
    try:
        rclpy.spin(node)
    except KeyboardInterrupt:
        pass
    finally:
        node.destroy_node()
        if rclpy.ok():
            rclpy.shutdown()

    main()

lessons.title: Knobs on the Outside
lessons.goal: Declare a parameter with a default and read its value inside the node.
lessons.theory:
A **parameter** is a named value owned by a node and settable from outside it. Anything a field engineer might want to change without editing code is a parameter: the maximum speed, the serial port of the laser, the frame id to publish in.

ROS 2 requires you to declare parameters before use. `self.declare_parameter('max_speed', 0.5)` registers the name and the default, and from then on the node exposes it in the graph. Reading is `self.get_parameter('max_speed').value`. Read an undeclared parameter and you get a `ParameterNotDeclaredException`, which is the system telling you to document your configuration surface.

The default matters. It is what runs when no launch file and no yaml file said otherwise, so it has to be the safe value. For a speed limit the safe default is slow, not the value you happened to be testing with.
lessons.task: Declare `max_speed` with a default of 0.5 and log the value the node actually started with.
lessons.hint: get_parameter returns a Parameter object, the value you want is in its value attribute.

lessons.title: Types Are Not Suggestions
lessons.goal: Declare parameters of several types and read them without losing the type.
lessons.theory:
A parameter has one of a fixed set of types: bool, integer, double, string, byte array, bool array, integer array, double array, string array. The type is fixed at declaration, inferred from the default you give.

The trap is the numeric literal. `self.declare_parameter('max_speed', 1)` declares an integer, and a later attempt to set it to `0.35` from a yaml file is rejected with a type error. Writing `1.0` declares a double. This costs people whole evenings, and the fix is one character.

The numbers come from the hardware, not from taste. The laser on this robot talks at 115200 bits per second, so `baud` is a whole count of bits and is declared as an integer, while a speed limit is a physical quantity and is declared as a double.

The port comes from the hardware too, and it is a string. On Linux a USB to serial adapter appears as a device file, and the first one the kernel finds is `/dev/ttyUSB0`. The trailing number is only the order of appearance, so a second adapter becomes `ttyUSB1`, and a board with native USB registers as `/dev/ttyACM0` instead. The path moves from bench to robot, which is precisely why it belongs in a parameter and not in a constant.

Declaring a parameter with `None` as default and no descriptor is an error in modern rclpy, because there is no way to infer the type. If a parameter is genuinely mandatory, declare it with `ParameterDescriptor(dynamic_typing=True)` or declare a sentinel default and refuse to start when it has not been overridden.
lessons.task: Declare the port as a string defaulting to `/dev/ttyUSB0`, the baud rate as an integer at 115200, the speed limit as a double and a debug flag as a bool, then log all four.

lessons.title: Fences Around the Knobs
lessons.goal: Attach a ParameterDescriptor with a range and a description to a parameter.
lessons.theory:
A bare declaration accepts any value of the right type, including a speed limit of 40 m/s on a robot that tips over at 1.2. A `ParameterDescriptor` lets you state the constraint so the middleware enforces it before your code sees the value.

`FloatingPointRange(from_value=0.0, to_value=1.2, step=0.0)` inside `descriptor.floating_point_range` bounds a double. `IntegerRange` does the same for integers. The `description` field is free text and shows up in `ros2 param describe`, which turns a parameter list into documentation.

`read_only=True` marks a parameter that can only be set at startup. Use it for the serial port and the frame id, things a node reads once when it opens the device. Attempting to change a read only parameter at runtime is rejected instead of silently ignored, which is the behaviour you want.

lessons.title: Guarding the Change
lessons.goal: Validate parameter changes at runtime with a set parameters callback.
lessons.theory:
Ranges cover numeric bounds. Everything else is your job. `self.add_on_set_parameters_callback(self.on_set)` registers a function that runs before any change is applied, receives the list of proposed `Parameter` objects, and returns a `SetParametersResult`.

Return `successful=False` with a reason and the change is rejected, the node keeps the old value and the caller sees the reason. This is where you refuse a speed increase while the robot is carrying a load, or reject a frame id that is not in the TF tree.

The callback must not have side effects that assume the change happened, because it runs before the value is stored. Apply the change by reading the parameter afterwards, or by caching the new value only on the successful path. Doing real work inside the callback also blocks the caller, so keep it to validation.

lessons.title: The Configuration Sheet

lessons.theory:
A parameter yaml file has a shape that is easy to get wrong. The top level key is the fully qualified node name, then a literal `ros__parameters` key, then the values. The double underscore is not a typo.

A node in a namespace needs its namespace in the key: `/front/laser_driver:` and not `laser_driver:`. The wildcard `/**:` applies to every node, which is how you set `use_sim_time` once for a whole robot instead of thirty times.

Nested keys become dotted parameter names. A block `serial:` with `port:` under it declares the parameter `serial.port`, and your node must declare exactly that name. The file is loaded with `--ros-args --params-file config/pilot.yaml` or from a launch file, and a key that matches no declared parameter is silently ignored, which is the reason a misspelled entry looks like the file was not loaded at all.

`ros2 param set /pilot max_speed 0.3` changes the value on a running robot and prints whether it was accepted, which is your validator from lesson four answering. This is the fastest tuning loop that exists in ROS 2: change, watch, change again, no rebuild.

`ros2 param dump /pilot` prints the current values in the yaml format of the previous lesson. The workflow that works: tune live until the robot behaves, dump to a file, commit the file. Tuning that only lives in your shell history is tuning you will do again next week.

lessons.title: Promises About Delivery
lessons.goal: Build a QoSProfile with best effort reliability for a high rate sensor stream.
lessons.theory:
Quality of Service is the contract between a publisher and a subscriber. The depth number you have been passing to `create_publisher` is a shortcut for a default profile. The full form is a `QoSProfile` object.

`ReliabilityPolicy.RELIABLE` retransmits until the message arrives. That is right for `cmd_vel`, a command you cannot afford to lose. `ReliabilityPolicy.BEST_EFFORT` sends once and moves on. That is right for a camera at 30 Hz over wifi, where a retransmitted frame arrives too late to be useful and only clogs the link.

The rule that surprises everyone: a best effort publisher and a reliable subscriber are **incompatible** and simply do not connect. No error, no data. Sensor drivers commonly publish best effort, so a subscriber written with the default reliable profile receives nothing, and this is the single most common cause of an empty `ros2 topic echo`.

lessons.title: Messages That Wait
lessons.goal: Use transient local durability so late subscribers still receive the last message.
lessons.theory:
`DurabilityPolicy.VOLATILE`, the default, means a subscriber that joins after a message was published never sees it. For a stream that is correct. For a map published once at startup it is a disaster: any node that starts thirty seconds later has no map and no way to ask for one.

`DurabilityPolicy.TRANSIENT_LOCAL` makes the publisher keep the last `depth` messages and deliver them to every new subscriber on connection. This is the ROS 2 replacement for what ROS 1 called a latched topic. `/map`, `/robot_description` and `/tf_static` all use it.

Both sides must agree, with the same asymmetry as reliability: a volatile publisher cannot satisfy a transient local subscriber, so they do not connect. When you publish a one shot topic, set transient local on the publisher and document it, because every consumer has to match.
lessons.task: Publish the map once with a transient local, reliable profile of depth 1 so any node that starts later still receives it.
lessons.solution:
import rclpy
from nav_msgs.msg import OccupancyGrid
from rclpy.node import Node
from rclpy.qos import DurabilityPolicy, QoSProfile, ReliabilityPolicy


class MapServer(Node):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('map_server')
        latched = QoSProfile(
            reliability=ReliabilityPolicy.RELIABLE,
            durability=DurabilityPolicy.TRANSIENT_LOCAL,
            depth=1,
        )
        self.pub = self.create_publisher(OccupancyGrid, 'map', latched)
        self.pub.publish(OccupancyGrid())
        self.get_logger().info('map published as transient local, late joiners will get it')


def main():

    except KeyboardInterrupt:

lessons.title: How Deep the Queue
lessons.goal: Choose history and depth so a slow subscriber drops old data instead of lagging.
lessons.theory:
`HistoryPolicy.KEEP_LAST` with a `depth` keeps a ring buffer of that many messages. `HistoryPolicy.KEEP_ALL` keeps everything the middleware can hold, bounded by DDS resource limits rather than by you.

Depth is a latency decision, not a memory decision. A subscriber with depth 50 on a 30 Hz camera that cannot keep up will process frames that are more than a second old, and a robot reacting to a second old image is a robot that has already hit the box. Depth 1 on that same topic means it always works on the newest frame and drops the rest, which is what a perception pipeline wants.

The opposite case is a command queue you must not lose, a sequence of waypoints for example. There KEEP_ALL or a generous depth is right, and the cost of buffering is acceptable because the data does not go stale.
lessons.task: Subscribe to the camera with a best effort profile of depth 1 so the callback always works on the newest frame.
lessons.hint: KEEP_LAST with depth 1 is the profile that always leaves you the newest message.

lessons.title: When the Stream Goes Quiet
lessons.goal: Detect a missing publisher with a QoS deadline and its event callback.
lessons.theory:
A **deadline** is a promise about rate. Setting `deadline=Duration(seconds=0.2)` on a subscription says you expect a message at least every 200 ms. When one does not arrive, the middleware calls your deadline missed event handler. You did not have to write a watchdog timer, DDS did it.

Events are wired with `SubscriptionEventCallbacks`, passed as `event_callbacks` to `create_subscription`. Besides `deadline`, there is `incompatible_qos`, which fires when a publisher exists but its profile cannot satisfy yours. That callback turns the silent non connection of the last three lessons into a logged explanation.

`liveliness` and `lifespan` complete the set: liveliness detects a publisher that is alive but has stopped asserting itself, lifespan discards messages older than a given age. On a robot with a safety controller, a deadline on the laser subscription is what stops the base when the sensor stops talking.

import rclpy
from rclpy.duration import Duration
from rclpy.node import Node
from rclpy.qos import QoSProfile, ReliabilityPolicy
from rclpy.qos_event import SubscriptionEventCallbacks
from sensor_msgs.msg import LaserScan


class Safety(Node):

            deadline=Duration(seconds=0.2),

        pass

lessons.goal: Write a Python launch file that starts several nodes at once.
lessons.theory:
A robot is a dozen nodes. Starting them by hand in a dozen terminals is not a workflow, it is a memory test. A **launch file** describes the whole system and starts it with one command.

ROS 2 launch files are Python. The file lives in `launch/` inside a package and must define `generate_launch_description()` returning a `LaunchDescription`. Inside it you put actions, and the most common action is `launch_ros.actions.Node`, which takes `package`, `executable` and usually `name`.

Run it with `ros2 launch nebula_bringup base.launch.py`. Every node's output is merged into your terminal, and Ctrl-C shuts all of them down in order. Being Python, a launch file can branch and loop, which is how a two arm robot launches the same driver twice from a for loop.

lessons.goal: Pass parameters to a node from a launch file, inline and from a yaml file.

The `parameters` argument of a `Node` action takes a list. Each element is either a dictionary of inline values or a path to a yaml file. They are applied in order, so a later entry overrides an earlier one, which is how you load a base configuration and then override one value for a test.

The path to the yaml file must be resolved, not guessed. `os.path.join(get_package_share_directory('nebula_bringup'), 'config', 'pilot.yaml')` finds the installed copy. Pointing at the source folder works on your machine and fails on the robot, where only `install/` exists.

For the yaml to be installed at all, `setup.py` needs a `data_files` entry that copies the `config` folder into the share directory. Forgetting that is the reason a launch file that worked yesterday fails with a missing file after a clean build.

lessons.theory:
Hardcoding a value in a launch file means editing the file to change it. `DeclareLaunchArgument('max_speed', default_value='0.5')` creates a switch that the operator sets on the command line: `ros2 launch nebula_bringup base.launch.py max_speed:=0.3`.

Reading it back is `LaunchConfiguration('max_speed')`. That object is not a string, it is a substitution resolved when the description is executed. You cannot do arithmetic with it or compare it with `==` in plain Python, you can only pass it where a substitution is accepted, which includes parameter values, node names and namespaces.

Always give a `default_value` and a `description`. `ros2 launch nebula_bringup base.launch.py --show-args` prints them, and that listing is the operating manual of your robot.

lessons.title: Twins on the Same Base
lessons.goal: Run the same node twice under different namespaces with remapped topics.
lessons.theory:
This is where relative topic names from chapter 2 pay off. A `Node` action takes `namespace`, and every relative name inside that node is pushed under it. The same laser driver launched with `namespace='front'` and `namespace='rear'` produces `/front/scan` and `/rear/scan` with zero code changes.

`remappings` handles the rest. It takes a list of pairs, `[('cmd_vel', 'cmd_vel_raw')]`, rewiring one name without touching the others. The classic use is inserting a safety filter: the pilot publishes to `cmd_vel_raw`, the filter reads that and publishes the real `cmd_vel`, and neither node knew about the other.

Node names must stay unique inside a namespace but may repeat across namespaces. Two nodes both called `laser_driver`, one in `/front` and one in `/rear`, are two distinct entries in the graph and every tool handles them correctly.
lessons.task: Launch two laser drivers, one in the `front` namespace and one in `rear`, and remap the pilot output from cmd_vel to cmd_vel_raw.
lessons.hint: namespace is a keyword of the Node action and remappings takes a list of from and to pairs.

lessons.title: Stacking the Descriptions
lessons.goal: Include one launch file from another and pass arguments through.
lessons.theory:
A real robot has one launch file per subsystem and one that ties them together. `IncludeLaunchDescription` pulls in another file, so `robot.launch.py` can include `base.launch.py`, `sensors.launch.py` and `navigation.launch.py`.

The include needs a source. `PythonLaunchDescriptionSource(os.path.join(share, 'launch', 'base.launch.py'))` points at an installed launch file, which again means `setup.py` must install the `launch` folder into the share directory.

`launch_arguments` passes values down as a list of pairs of strings, `[('max_speed', '0.3')]`. Arguments do not inherit automatically: a child file only receives what the parent hands it, which is a feature, because it keeps each subsystem's interface explicit instead of relying on a global soup of values.
