lessons.title: Reacting to the Launch
lessons.goal: Run a process at startup and react to its exit with an event handler.
lessons.theory:
Not everything in a launch file is a node. `ExecuteProcess` runs any command, which is how you start `ros2 bag record` alongside a test, or call a calibration script before the drivers come up.

`RegisterEventHandler` with `OnProcessExit` fires an action when a process ends. The usual pattern is sequencing: run the calibration process, and only when it exits successfully start the driver that depends on the calibration file. Launch has no built in ordering otherwise, everything starts at once.

The other handler worth knowing is `OnProcessStart`. Together they let a launch file express a small state machine. When the logic gets bigger than that, the right answer is a lifecycle node and a supervisor, which is where the rest of this chapter goes.
lessons.task: Record the three topics with ExecuteProcess and log a line when the recorder exits.
lessons.hint: ExecuteProcess takes cmd as a list of strings, and the handler needs the action object as its target.

lessons.title: States Before Motion
lessons.goal: Describe the managed lifecycle states and the transitions between them.
lessons.theory:
A plain node starts doing its job the moment its constructor runs. For a laser driver that means opening a serial port during construction, and if the port is missing the process dies before anything can react. A **lifecycle node** separates existence from activity.

The states are `unconfigured`, `inactive`, `active` and `finalized`. The transitions between them are `configure`, `activate`, `deactivate`, `cleanup` and `shutdown`. A node starts unconfigured, `configure` allocates resources and opens devices, `activate` starts publishing, `deactivate` stops publishing while keeping the device open.

The value is deterministic startup. A supervisor can configure every node, check that all of them reached `inactive`, and only then activate them, so the robot never runs with half its sensors. It is also how you restart one driver without restarting the process.
lessons.task: Complete the transition table so every transition maps to the state it leads to, keeping the lookup at the bottom working.
lessons.solution:
TRANSITIONS = {
    'configure': 'inactive',
    'activate': 'active',
    'deactivate': 'inactive',
    'cleanup': 'unconfigured',
    'shutdown': 'finalized',
}

print(TRANSITIONS.get('activate', 'unknown'))
lessons.hint: Deactivate and configure both land in the same state, and shutdown is the only one way door.

lessons.title: The Managed Driver
lessons.goal: Implement a LifecycleNode with on_configure, on_activate and on_deactivate.
lessons.theory:
`rclpy.lifecycle.LifecycleNode` is the base class. You override the transition callbacks, each receiving the previous state and returning `TransitionCallbackReturn.SUCCESS`, `FAILURE` or `ERROR`. Returning failure keeps the node in the old state and the supervisor learns the driver could not open its port.

The division of work is strict. `on_configure` allocates: create publishers, open the serial device, read parameters. `on_activate` starts the flow: enable the timer, call `super().on_activate` so lifecycle publishers begin sending. `on_deactivate` stops the flow but keeps the resources. `on_cleanup` releases what configure allocated.

A `LifecyclePublisher`, created with `create_lifecycle_publisher`, silently drops messages while the node is inactive. That is the safety property that makes the whole design worth it: an inactive driver cannot accidentally publish a stale scan into a live navigation stack.
lessons.task: Complete the driver so configure creates the lifecycle publisher and the timer, activate starts it and deactivate stops it, each returning SUCCESS.
lessons.hint: Create the timer in configure and cancel it immediately, then reset it in activate.

lessons.title: Driving the States
lessons.goal: Trigger lifecycle transitions from the command line and from a launch file.
lessons.theory:
A lifecycle node exposes services for its transitions. `ros2 lifecycle list /managed_laser` shows what is available from the current state, `ros2 lifecycle get /managed_laser` prints the state, and `ros2 lifecycle set /managed_laser configure` performs a transition.

From a launch file you use `launch_ros.actions.LifecycleNode` instead of `Node`, then `EmitEvent` with `ChangeState` to request a transition, usually chained with `RegisterEventHandler` and `OnStateTransition` so activate only fires once configure succeeded.

On a real robot this chain is written once in a bringup launch file and never touched again: configure everything, verify all reached inactive, activate in dependency order, sensors before estimators before behaviour. That is the whole reason lifecycle exists, and it is what the final chapter of this course builds.
lessons.task: Build the three command lines that read the state of the managed laser, configure it and then activate it.
lessons.hint: One get and two sets, and the transition name is the last token of the line.

lessons.title: Every Number Has a Home
lessons.goal: Explain the TF2 tree and name the standard frames of a mobile robot.
lessons.theory:
A distance of 1.2 metres is meaningless on its own. It is 1.2 metres from the laser, which sits 18 cm above and 10 cm in front of the wheel axis, on a robot that is somewhere in a room. **TF2** is the system that keeps all those relationships and lets you convert a measurement from one frame to another at a given time.

TF2 is a tree, not a graph. Every frame has exactly one parent, and there are no cycles. The convention on a mobile robot is `map` to `odom` to `base_link` to the sensor frames. Odometry publishes `odom` to `base_link`, localisation publishes `map` to `odom` as the correction, and the sensors hang off `base_link` with fixed offsets.

One parent per frame is the rule people break first. If both odometry and localisation publish a transform whose child is `base_link`, the tree is broken and lookups return whichever arrived last. The corrections go on the other side, which is why `map` to `odom` exists at all.
lessons.task: Complete the parent table so the body, the laser and the imu each hang off the right frame, keeping the lookup at the bottom working.

    'odom': 'map',
    'base_link': 'odom',
    'laser_link': 'base_link',
    'imu_link': 'base_link',
}

print(PARENT.get('base_link', 'unknown'))
lessons.hint: Sensors hang off the body, the body hangs off odometry, odometry hangs off the map.

lessons.title: Bolted in Place
lessons.goal: Publish a fixed sensor offset with a StaticTransformBroadcaster.
lessons.theory:
A laser bolted to the chassis never moves relative to it. Publishing that transform at 50 Hz would waste bandwidth forever. `StaticTransformBroadcaster` publishes it once on `/tf_static`, a transient local topic, so every node that starts later still receives it.

The message is a `geometry_msgs/TransformStamped`. `header.frame_id` is the parent, `child_frame_id` is the child, `transform.translation` is the offset in metres and `transform.rotation` is a quaternion. A quaternion of all zeros is invalid and TF2 will reject it, the identity rotation is `w = 1.0`.

Send it once, from the constructor, with `broadcaster.sendTransform(tf)`, and keep the broadcaster alive on `self`. That method kept its C++ spelling when tf2 was wrapped for Python, so it is `sendTransform` and not `send_transform`, and it takes either one message or a list of them. Because the topic is latched, there is no race with subscribers that start afterwards, which is exactly why static transforms use a different mechanism from dynamic ones.

lessons.title: The Moving Body
lessons.goal: Broadcast a changing odom to base_link transform on every odometry update.
lessons.theory:
The pose of the robot changes, so its transform has to be republished continuously. `TransformBroadcaster` sends on `/tf`, and the usual rate is whatever your odometry produces, 20 to 50 Hz on a wheeled base. Every `geometry_msgs/msg/TransformStamped` names its edge with two strings, the parent in `header.frame_id` and the child in `child_frame_id`, and TF2 builds the tree out of those two names alone.

The stamp is the critical field. It must be the time the pose was valid, taken from the node clock, not the time you happened to publish. TF2 interpolates between transforms using those stamps, so a wrong stamp silently distorts every lookup that crosses this edge.

A planar robot still needs a full quaternion. From a yaw angle it is `z = sin(yaw / 2)` and `w = cos(yaw / 2)`, with `x` and `y` at zero. Publishing yaw in the `z` field of the rotation as if it were an Euler angle is a mistake that produces a robot that spins in RViz while driving straight in reality.
lessons.task: Broadcast odom to base_link at 20 Hz using the stored x, y and yaw, converting the yaw into a quaternion.

lessons.title: Asking the Tree
lessons.goal: Look up a transform between two frames with a Buffer and a TransformListener.
lessons.theory:
To read the tree you need two objects: a `Buffer`, which stores the last few seconds of transforms, and a `TransformListener`, which fills that buffer from `/tf` and `/tf_static`. Create both in the constructor and keep both on `self`.

`buffer.lookup_transform(target_frame, source_frame, time)` answers the question. The argument order reads backwards until you internalise it: it returns the transform that takes data **from** the source frame **into** the target frame. `lookup_transform('base_link', 'laser_link', ...)` gives you what you need to move a laser point into the body frame.

Passing `rclpy.time.Time()`, a zero time, means the latest available transform. That is the pragmatic choice for a live robot. Passing a real stamp asks for the transform at that instant and is what you want when transforming stamped data, at the cost of having to handle the case where the buffer does not have it yet.
lessons.task: Look up the latest transform from `laser_link` into `base_link` once per second and log the translation, handling a failed lookup.
lessons.hint: Target frame first, source second, and TransformException covers every failure mode of the lookup.

lessons.title: Moving a Measurement
lessons.goal: Transform a stamped point into another frame and handle extrapolation errors.
lessons.theory:
Looking up a transform is half the job. `tf2_geometry_msgs` adds the other half: `buffer.transform(point_stamped, 'base_link')` takes a stamped message and returns it expressed in the target frame, using the stamp inside the message to pick the right moment in the tree.

The import looks unused and is not. `import tf2_geometry_msgs` registers the conversion functions for `PointStamped`, `PoseStamped` and friends. Without it the call raises a type error that says nothing about a missing import, and linters that remove unused imports break TF2 code regularly.

`ExtrapolationException` is the error you will meet most. It means the buffer holds transforms around that time but not at it, usually because the data is a few milliseconds newer than the last transform. The standard fix is `timeout=Duration(seconds=0.1)` on the call, which waits for the transform to arrive instead of failing immediately.

lessons.title: The Body Written Down
lessons.goal: Describe a robot in URDF with links, a fixed joint and a continuous joint.
lessons.theory:
**URDF** is the XML that describes the physical robot: which parts exist, where they sit, how they are connected. Two element types carry everything. A `<link>` is a rigid body with visual, collision and inertial blocks. A `<joint>` connects a parent link to a child link and says how they may move.

Joint types you need on a mobile base: `fixed` for anything bolted on, `continuous` for a wheel that spins without limit, `revolute` for a joint with limits, `prismatic` for a slide. The `<origin>` inside a joint places the child relative to the parent, in metres and radians, and `<axis>` names the axis of motion as a unit vector in the child frame, three numbers in x y z order. A wheel standing upright on a mobile base turns about its own y axis, which is written `<axis xyz="0 1 0"/>`.

URDF is what generates the TF2 tree. Every joint becomes a transform, fixed joints become static transforms, moving joints become dynamic ones driven by the joint states. Getting the origins right in the URDF is the same work as getting the frames right in TF2, done once.

lessons.title: One Description, Two Wheels
lessons.goal: Factor repeated URDF into a xacro macro with parameters.
lessons.theory:
A four wheeled robot written in plain URDF is the same twenty lines four times, with one number different. **xacro** is the macro language that fixes that. The file becomes `robot.urdf.xacro`, declares the namespace `xmlns:xacro`, and is expanded before anything reads it.

`<xacro:property name="wheel_radius" value="0.05"/>` defines a constant, used as `${wheel_radius}`. Arithmetic works inside the braces, so `${wheel_radius * 2}` is valid. `<xacro:macro name="wheel" params="prefix reflect">` defines a reusable block, and `<xacro:wheel prefix="left" reflect="1"/>` instantiates it.

Expand it with `xacro robot.urdf.xacro > robot.urdf` to see what it produced, which is the only sane way to debug a macro. In a launch file you use the `Command` substitution to expand it at startup so the source of truth stays the xacro file.

lessons.title: From Description to Frames
lessons.goal: Launch robot_state_publisher so the URDF becomes live TF frames.
lessons.theory:
`robot_state_publisher` is the node that turns a URDF into transforms. You give it the description as the `robot_description` parameter, it publishes every fixed joint on `/tf_static` and computes the moving joints from `/joint_states`.

The description reaches it through the `Command` substitution: `Command(['xacro ', path])` runs xacro at launch time and puts the resulting XML in the parameter. Wrapping it in `ParameterValue(..., value_type=str)` is required, otherwise launch tries to guess the type and can turn the XML into something else.

The moving joints need someone to publish `sensor_msgs/JointState`. On a real robot that is the motor controller reporting encoder positions. Without a publisher, `robot_state_publisher` warns that it has no joint states and the wheels stay frozen in RViz while the base moves, which is the usual first symptom.

lessons.title: A World to Crash In
lessons.goal: Spawn the robot in Gazebo and bridge the simulated topics into ROS 2.
lessons.theory:
Gazebo runs the physics. It is a separate process with its own transport, and the two worlds meet through `ros_gz_bridge`. Nothing crosses that boundary unless you bridge it explicitly, which is why a freshly spawned robot appears in the simulator and publishes nothing to ROS 2.

`ros_gz_sim create -topic robot_description` spawns the robot from the description already published by `robot_state_publisher`, so simulation and reality share one source of truth. The `parameter_bridge` then maps topic pairs with a type spec such as `/scan@sensor_msgs/msg/LaserScan[gz.msgs.LaserScan`, where the bracket direction says which way the data flows.

The piece people forget is the clock. Bridge `/clock`, which carries a `rosgraph_msgs/msg/Clock`, and launch every node with `use_sim_time` true, otherwise your nodes timestamp with wall time while the simulator runs at a different rate, and TF2 rejects everything as extrapolation into the future.

lessons.goal: Decide the node split, the topics and the channel of each interaction for a complete robot.
lessons.theory:
The project of this chapter is a full differential drive robot in ROS 2: a laser, wheel odometry, a safety layer, a behaviour that drives to a target, and a supervisor that brings everything up in order. Every piece is a node, and the design work is deciding where the boundaries go.

The rule that has held up for twenty years of robots: one node per resource or per responsibility. The laser driver owns the serial port. The odometry node owns the encoder integration. The safety filter owns the final word on `cmd_vel`. Merging two of those saves a file and costs you the ability to restart one without the other.

Write the contract before the code. Every edge in your design is a topic name, a type and a rate, or a service, or an action. That table is the architecture, and a mistake in it is far cheaper to fix now than after five nodes assume it.

lessons.title: The Eye That Reports
lessons.goal: Write the laser driver node with parameters, sensor QoS and a stamped message.
lessons.theory:
The first node of the robot is the sensor driver, and it puts together most of what this course covered. It reads its port and frame from parameters, publishes with a best effort sensor profile, stamps every message with the node clock and names the frame it measured from. `self.get_clock().now()` hands back an `rclpy.time.Time`, while the header field is a `builtin_interfaces/msg/Time`, so the clock reading goes through `to_msg()` before it fits.

That sensor profile is a `QoSProfile` whose reliability is `rclpy.qos.ReliabilityPolicy.BEST_EFFORT`: each scan is sent once and never retransmitted, which is what a scanner running at 10 Hz wants, because a beam resent late is already useless and only steals bandwidth from the next one. The other half of the pair, `ReliabilityPolicy.RELIABLE`, belongs on commands and on anything a node cannot afford to miss, never on a high rate sensor stream.

The driver publishes and nothing else. It does not filter, it does not decide, it does not stop the robot. That discipline is what lets you replace it with a Gazebo bridge or a bag replay without any other node noticing, which is the whole promise of the topic abstraction.

One detail from the real world: fill `angle_min`, `angle_max`, `angle_increment`, `range_min` and `range_max` honestly. Downstream code computes beam indices from those fields, and a driver that leaves them at zero produces a division by zero in every consumer.

lessons.title: Knowing Where You Are
lessons.goal: Write the odometry node that publishes nav_msgs/Odometry and the matching TF.
lessons.theory:
The odometry node integrates wheel velocities into a pose and tells the rest of the system two things at once: a `nav_msgs/Odometry` message on `/odom` for anything that wants the pose with covariance, and a transform from `odom` to `base_link` handed to TF2 through `TransformBroadcaster.sendTransform()`, camelCase in Python as well.

Both have to agree, on the same stamp, from the same integration step. Publishing the message from one timer and the transform from another produces a robot whose drawn pose lags its computed pose, and every transformed laser point lands slightly wrong.

The integration itself for a differential base: `x += v * cos(yaw) * dt`, `y += v * sin(yaw) * dt`, `yaw += w * dt`. It drifts, that is expected, correcting it is the job of localisation publishing `map` to `odom`. Odometry must never try to be right in the world frame, only smooth and continuous in its own.

import math

import rclpy
from geometry_msgs.msg import TransformStamped, Twist
from nav_msgs.msg import Odometry
from rclpy.node import Node
from tf2_ros import TransformBroadcaster


class OdometryNode(Node):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('odometry')
        self.pub = self.create_publisher(Odometry, 'odom', 10)
        self.broadcaster = TransformBroadcaster(self)
        self.sub = self.create_subscription(Twist, 'cmd_vel', self.on_cmd, 10)
        self.v = 0.0
        self.w = 0.0
        self.x = 0.0
        self.y = 0.0
        self.yaw = 0.0
        self.dt = 0.05
        self.timer = self.create_timer(self.dt, self.on_tick)

    def on_cmd(self, msg):
        self.v = msg.linear.x
        self.w = msg.angular.z

    def on_tick(self):
        self.x += self.v * math.cos(self.yaw) * self.dt
        self.y += self.v * math.sin(self.yaw) * self.dt
        self.yaw += self.w * self.dt
        stamp = self.get_clock().now().to_msg()
        qz = math.sin(self.yaw / 2.0)
        qw = math.cos(self.yaw / 2.0)

        odom = Odometry()
        odom.header.stamp = stamp
        odom.header.frame_id = 'odom'
        odom.child_frame_id = 'base_link'
        odom.pose.pose.position.x = self.x
        odom.pose.pose.position.y = self.y
        odom.pose.pose.orientation.z = qz
        odom.pose.pose.orientation.w = qw
        odom.twist.twist.linear.x = self.v
        odom.twist.twist.angular.z = self.w
        self.pub.publish(odom)

        tf = TransformStamped()
        tf.header.stamp = stamp
        tf.header.frame_id = 'odom'
        tf.child_frame_id = 'base_link'
        tf.transform.translation.x = self.x
        tf.transform.translation.y = self.y
        tf.transform.rotation.z = qz
        tf.transform.rotation.w = qw
        self.broadcaster.sendTransform(tf)


def main():
    rclpy.init()
    node = OdometryNode()
    try:
        rclpy.spin(node)
    except KeyboardInterrupt:
        pass
    finally:
        node.destroy_node()
        if rclpy.ok():
            rclpy.shutdown()

    main()

lessons.title: The Layer That Says No
lessons.goal: Write the safety filter that caps speed and blocks motion when an obstacle is close.
lessons.theory:
The safety node sits between the behaviour and the wheels. It subscribes to `cmd_vel_raw`, subscribes to `scan`, and publishes the real `cmd_vel`. Nothing else may publish `cmd_vel`, and that is enforced by the launch file through remappings rather than by convention.

It does two jobs. It caps the commanded speed at the `max_speed` parameter, so no behaviour can ever ask for more than the hardware tolerates. And it zeroes forward motion when the nearest forward reading is below the stop distance, while still allowing rotation so the robot can turn away from what it is facing.

A safety layer must fail closed. If no scan has arrived for half a second, it must publish zero rather than trust the last reading. A filter that only blocks when it sees an obstacle is not a safety layer, it is an optimist.

import rclpy
from geometry_msgs.msg import Twist
from rclpy.node import Node
from rclpy.qos import QoSProfile, ReliabilityPolicy
from sensor_msgs.msg import LaserScan


class SafetyFilter(Node):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('safety_filter')
        self.declare_parameter('max_speed', 0.5)
        self.declare_parameter('stop_distance', 0.4)
        sensor_qos = QoSProfile(reliability=ReliabilityPolicy.BEST_EFFORT, depth=5)
        self.pub = self.create_publisher(Twist, 'cmd_vel', 10)
        self.create_subscription(LaserScan, 'scan', self.on_scan, sensor_qos)
        self.create_subscription(Twist, 'cmd_vel_raw', self.on_command, 10)
        self.nearest = math.inf
        self.last_scan = self.get_clock().now()

    def on_scan(self, msg):
        valid = [r for r in msg.ranges if math.isfinite(r)]
        self.nearest = min(valid) if valid else math.inf
        self.last_scan = self.get_clock().now()

    def on_command(self, msg):
        out = Twist()
        age = (self.get_clock().now() - self.last_scan).nanoseconds / 1e9
        if age > 0.5:
            self.get_logger().error('scan is {:.2f} s old, blocking motion'.format(age), throttle_duration_sec=2.0)
            self.pub.publish(out)
            return
        limit = self.get_parameter('max_speed').value
        stop_distance = self.get_parameter('stop_distance').value
        forward = max(-limit, min(limit, msg.linear.x))
        if self.nearest < stop_distance and forward > 0.0:
            self.get_logger().warn('obstacle at {:.2f} m, holding'.format(self.nearest), throttle_duration_sec=1.0)
            forward = 0.0
        out.linear.x = forward
        out.angular.z = msg.angular.z
        self.pub.publish(out)


def main():
    rclpy.init()
    node = SafetyFilter()
    try:
        rclpy.spin(node)
    except KeyboardInterrupt:
        pass
    finally:
        node.destroy_node()
        if rclpy.ok():
            rclpy.shutdown()

    main()

lessons.title: The Errand That Drives
lessons.goal: Write the behaviour action server that drives a distance with feedback and cancellation.
lessons.theory:
The behaviour node is the only one that decides where the robot goes. It offers the `drive_distance` action, reads `/odom` to know how far it has come, and publishes to `cmd_vel_raw` so the safety filter always gets the last word.

Stepping the goal from a timer instead of looping inside the execute callback is what makes it responsive. The callback accepts the goal, stores the handle and the target, and returns. The timer publishes the velocity, sends progress with `publish_feedback` on the goal handle, reads `is_cancel_requested` on that same handle and finishes the goal when the distance is reached. Nothing blocks, so the node keeps answering while it drives.

When the goal ends, for any reason, publish a zero Twist. Succeeded, cancelled or aborted, the wheels stop. A behaviour that only stops on success is the one that drives into a wall the day a goal is cancelled.

lessons.title: The Hand on the Switch
lessons.goal: Write a supervisor node that configures and activates the managed nodes in order.
lessons.theory:
The supervisor is the node that decides the robot is ready. It calls the lifecycle services of the managed nodes: `configure` on all of them, wait for each to reach inactive, then `activate` in dependency order, sensors first, then estimators, then behaviour.

The service is `/<node>/change_state`, of type `lifecycle_msgs/srv/ChangeState`, and the transition id comes from `lifecycle_msgs/msg/Transition`. `TRANSITION_CONFIGURE` and `TRANSITION_ACTIVATE` are the two you need. The reply carries a boolean, and a false there means the node refused, most often because a device is missing. `call_async(request)` returns a future straight away and `rclpy.spin_until_future_complete` is what waits on it, because the blocking `call` deadlocks the executor when it runs inside a callback.

The supervisor is also where an operator level failure policy lives. If the laser cannot configure, it must not activate the behaviour, and it must say which node failed. That refusal is the difference between a robot that will not start and a robot that starts blind.
lessons.task: Complete the supervisor so it sends a transition to a named node asynchronously and reports whether the node accepted it.

import rclpy
from lifecycle_msgs.msg import Transition
from lifecycle_msgs.srv import ChangeState
from rclpy.node import Node


class Supervisor(Node):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('supervisor')
        self.managed = ['laser_driver', 'odometry', 'drive_behaviour']
        self.clients = {
            name: self.create_client(ChangeState, '/{}/change_state'.format(name))
            for name in self.managed
        }

    def transition(self, name, transition_id):
        client = self.clients[name]
        if not client.wait_for_service(timeout_sec=5.0):
            self.get_logger().error('{} has no lifecycle service'.format(name))
            return False
        request = ChangeState.Request()
        request.transition.id = transition_id
        future = client.call_async(request)
        rclpy.spin_until_future_complete(self, future, timeout_sec=5.0)
        response = future.result()
        if response is None or not response.success:
            self.get_logger().error('{} refused transition {}'.format(name, transition_id))
            return False
        self.get_logger().info('{} took transition {}'.format(name, transition_id))
        return True


def main():
    rclpy.init()
    node = Supervisor()
    for name in node.managed:
        node.transition(name, Transition.TRANSITION_CONFIGURE)
    for name in node.managed:
        node.transition(name, Transition.TRANSITION_ACTIVATE)
    node.destroy_node()
    rclpy.shutdown()


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()
lessons.hint: The transition id goes into request.transition.id, and the reply exposes success as a boolean.

The last piece is the launch file that starts the robot: the description through `robot_state_publisher`, the laser driver, the odometry node, the safety filter, the behaviour, and a bag recording of the three topics that matter. One command, one system.

The wiring lives here and nowhere else. The behaviour publishes `cmd_vel_raw`, the safety filter reads it and owns `cmd_vel`, so no remapping is needed if the nodes were written with the right relative names, which is what chapter 2 was for. A launch argument carries the speed limit down to the filter, and `use_sim_time` is set once for everyone.

When this file works, you have the whole course in one place: packages, nodes, topics, parameters, QoS, TF2, a URDF, an action, a lifecycle and a recording of the run to prove what happened. That is a ROS 2 robot, and everything else you will build is more of the same shape.

from launch import LaunchDescription
from launch.actions import DeclareLaunchArgument, ExecuteProcess
from launch.substitutions import LaunchConfiguration
from launch_ros.actions import Node


def generate_launch_description():
    max_speed = DeclareLaunchArgument(
        'max_speed',
        default_value='0.5',
        description='forward speed cap applied by the safety filter',
    )
    common = {'use_sim_time': True}

    laser = Node(
        package='nebula_bringup',
        executable='laser_driver',
        name='laser_driver',
        output='screen',
        parameters=[common, {'frame_id': 'laser_link'}],
    )
    odometry = Node(
        package='nebula_bringup',
        executable='odometry',
        name='odometry',
        output='screen',
        parameters=[common],
    )
    safety = Node(
        package='nebula_bringup',
        executable='safety_filter',
        name='safety_filter',
        output='screen',
        parameters=[common, {'max_speed': LaunchConfiguration('max_speed'), 'stop_distance': 0.4}],
    )
    behaviour = Node(
        package='nebula_bringup',
        executable='drive_behaviour',
        name='drive_behaviour',
        output='screen',
        parameters=[common],
    )
    recorder = ExecuteProcess(
        cmd=['ros2', 'bag', 'record', '-o', 'nebula_run', '/scan', '/odom', '/cmd_vel'],
        output='screen',
    )

    return LaunchDescription([max_speed, laser, odometry, safety, behaviour, recorder])
